  • Although trade volume increased slightly to 5.1 million tonnes in April 2026, it remained around 95.1% below pre-disruption levels, indicating that the Strait continued to operate far below its nor-mal capacity.

DetailedAnalysis_EN:

Total cargo volume stood at 97.5 m tonnes in Janu-ary 2026 and increased to 105.8 m tonnes in February 2026, reflecting an 8.5% month-on-month increase. This indicates that the Strait was still functioning normally before the conflict-related closure, with strong cargo movement across tank-ers, dry bulk vessels, container vessels, general cargo vessels, and roll-on/roll-off vessels.
  • The disruption became clearly visible in March 2026, when total transit trade volume collapsed to only 3.1 m tonnes, representing a decline of approximately 97.1% compared with February lev-els. The decline was broad-based across vessel categories rather than being limited to one shipping segment. Tanker volume fell sharply from 74.4 m tonnes in February to 1.3 m tonnes in March, a decline of approximately 98.3%. Container cargo volume declined from 13.8 m tonnes to 0.6 m tonnes, while dry bulk volume dropped from 16.7 m tonnes to 1.1 m tonnes. This confirms that the disruption affected the Straitâ€™s overall cargo movement capacity, not only energy-related shipping activity.
  • Although transit trade volume increased slightly to 5.1 m tonnes in April 2026, this should be interpreted as a limited rebound rather than a recovery. Compared with February 2026, total trade volume in April remained approximately 95.1% lower, indicating that the Strait continued to operate far below its normal capacity.Tanker volume also remained severely depressed at 2.7 m tonnes in April, around 96.4% below February levels. This suggests that only a small fraction of normal cargo movement capacity had been re-stored after the initial collapse in March.
  • For Qatar, the disruption represents a major export continuity risk. The sharp decline in tanker volume is especially significant because Qatarâ€™s strategic exports , including LNG/petroleum gases, ammonia, refined products, and chemical cargoes, rely heavily on tanker movement through the Strait.The decline in dry bulk and container-related volumes is also important because Qatarâ€™s fertilizers, sulphur, helium/rare gases, polymers, aluminum, and other industrial goods depend on Maritime cargo flows. Although the indicator is not Qatar-specific, the scale of the collapse through Hormuz strongly suggests severe pressure on Qatarâ€™s ability to maintain reliable seaborne export flows to global markets.

Summary_EN:
• Qatarâ€™s helium exports represent a strategic component of global advanced technology supply chains.
  • Exports are concentrated in major industrial economies, including France, the United States, Japan, China and Germany.
  • Helium is strategically important due to limited substitutes and its role in semiconductors, medical imaging, aerospace and scientific research.
  • The disruption of Qatari production, nearly one-third of global supply, shifted the helium market from a 15% surplus to a 15% deficit.
  • Despite greater logistical flexibility than LNG, regional and maritime constraints continue to pressure global helium supply stability.
  • U.S. supplies temporarily eased market diruptions, particularly for Asian semiconductor manufacturers, although impacts are expected to persist over the longer term.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Qatarâ€™s helium and rare gases exports under HS 2804 hold strategic importance despite being far smaller in value than LNG exports, due to their critical role in advanced industries such as semiconductors, aerospace, medical imaging, scientific research, and defense technologies. Export destinations, including France, the United States, Japan, China, Germany, and the UAE, reflect Qatarâ€™s integration into global industrial and technology supply chains.
  • According to Washington Post Intelligence, Qatar accounted for nearly 30% of global helium supply, making the market highly sensitive to disruptions in Qatari production. Before the regional conflict, the global helium market recorded an estimated 15% oversupply; however, the shutdown of Qatari production rapidly shifted the market into an estimated 15% deficit.
  • Washington Post Intelligence also highlighted the structural fragility of the helium market, as helium exists only in very low concentrations within natural gas fields. Concentrations range between 0.1% and 0.3% in U.S. fields and only 0.04% to 0.06% in Qatari fields, limiting the economic viability of rapidly expanding production capacity.
  • The data further show strong Asian dependence on Qatari helium. According to the Korea International Trade Association, cited by Washington Post Intelligence, South Korea imported nearly two-thirds of its helium needs from Qatar in 2025, This reflects the direct relationship between the stability of Qatari helium exports and the continuity of industrial production within Asian technology supply chains.
  • Furthermore, helium shipments from the Gulf region to South Korea require approximately one month in transit, meaning that any maritime or logistical disruption directly affects downstream manufacturing operations.
  • Washington Post Intelligence also indicated that U.S. helium supplies temporarily contributed to stabilizing the market. In early April, Linde and Air Products, both heavily dependent on U.S.-sourced helium, signed new long-term supply agreements with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. These agreements enabled semiconductor manufacturers to offset part of the lost Qatari supply and avoid immediate production disruptions in the short term. Nevertheless, the capacity of U.S. to compensate for the global shortfall remains structurally limited, as U.S. helium production itself is concentrated in only a few geological basins and facilities, particularly the Shute Creek Gas Processing Plant in Wyoming, which alone accounts for approximately 30% to 40% of total U.S. helium production.

Summary_EN:
Q1 2026 recorded a budget deficit of QR 10.3 billion â€” the largest single-quarter deficit in the observation period and more than seven times the previous worst quarter (QR 1.4 billion deficit in Q3 2025). Revenue fell to QR 38 billion while expenditure remained at approximately QR 48.3 billion, producing a gap that has no precedent in the 2024â€“2026 data. The State entered 2026 with its revenue base under severe pressure, driven by declining hydrocarbon income which funds approximately 88% of the budget.

The Strait of Hormuz Closure Impact Dashboard provides critical context: Qatar's LNG exports  the backbone of hydrocarbon revenue fell 7.39% to QR 12.88 billion in February 2026, and Strait transit trade volume collapsed to near-zero in April 2026. These signals indicate that the revenue pressure visible in the budget is not merely cyclical; it is directly linked to disruptions in Qatar's export delivery capacity.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
Expenditure at QR 48.3 billion in Q1 2026 is not unusually high â€” it is consistent with prior Q1 levels when adjusted for budget growth. The deficit is a revenue problem, not a spending problem. Chapters I and II (Salaries and Current Expenditure) are structurally fixed. Chapter IV (Major Capex) is the only lever available, but deferring capital investment to close an operating deficit carries its own long-term costs.
The Transit Trade Volume indicator collapsing from a baseline of ~90â€“120 million ton-km per month to just 5 million in April 2026, and vessel activity falling from ~2,500â€“3,000 to just 203. These two independent indicators confirm a near-total disruption of commercial shipping through the Strait. Since all of Qatar's hydrocarbon exports transit this route, a sustained closure means export deliveries stop â€” and a budget already showing a QR 10.3 billion deficit in Q1 2026 faces a far deeper shortfall in Q2 2026 if deliveries cannot resume.

The Commodity Price Index shows the sub-index Energy standing at 130.9 in March 2026, above the 2024 baseline. Higher energy prices partially support per-unit revenues â€” but only when volumes are being delivered. In a near-zero transit scenario, elevated prices provide no fiscal benefit. This indicator should not be read as an offset to the deficit; it is only relevant if export delivery resumes

Summary_EN:
atarâ€™s fertiliser and ammonia exports are a significant gas-linked industrial export stream and an important part of the countryâ€™s non-LNG export base. NPC trade data shows exports of around QAR 7.28bn in 2024 and QAR 8.53bn in 2025, confirming the sectorâ€™s continued commercial importance.

The current disruption should be viewed as both a production risk and an export-flow risk, as fertiliser and ammonia depend on gas-linked industrial operations and maritime access through the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz. While smaller than LNG in value, disruption to this sector can affect Qatarâ€™s industrial output, export diversification, and reliability with key recurring markets such as the USA, Singapore, India, Switzerland, UAE, and Japan.

Globally, reduced Qatari fertiliser and ammonia supply can tighten availability, support higher fertiliser prices, and create wider food-security pressure by increasing input costs for agriculture.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
Qatarâ€™s fertiliser and ammonia exports represent an important gas-linked industrial export stream, supporting non-LNG export earnings and Qatarâ€™s role in global agricultural input supply. Based on NPC trade data, Qatar exported around QAR 7.28bn in fertiliser and ammonia products in 2024, rising to around QAR 8.53bn in 2025. This confirms that the sector has remained commercially significant beyond LNG, with nitrogenous fertilisers and ammonia forming the core export base.

The current disruption should therefore be read as both a production shock and an export-flow shock. Fertiliser and ammonia production is closely linked to Qatarâ€™s gas-based industrial system, while export delivery depends heavily on maritime access through the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz. Any disruption to gas-linked operations, port activity, or shipping routes can reduce Qatarâ€™s ability to convert production capacity into export revenue, even where underlying demand remains strong.

For Qatar, the impact is smaller than LNG in absolute value, but still relevant for industrial output, export diversification, and non-hydrocarbon-linked revenue. The main risk is not only lost monthly export value, but the disruption of a reliable export channel to recurring markets such as the United States, Singapore, India, Switzerland, the UAE, and Japan. A prolonged disruption could weaken Qatarâ€™s position as a stable supplier and create short-term revenue leakage in an industrial segment that has shown strong recent performance.

Globally, the impact is broader because Qatar is part of the low-cost gas-based fertiliser supply chain. Disruption to Qatari urea and ammonia exports can tighten availability, support higher fertiliser prices, and increase cost pressures for agricultural importers. This creates a second-round food-security risk: higher fertiliser prices can reduce affordability, lower fertiliser application, and ultimately add pressure to food production costs and food prices.

Summary_EN: • The Online Service Index (OSI) is one of the key components of the E-Government Development Index (EGDI) developed by the United Nations, which also includes the Human Capital Index (HCI) and the Telecommunications Infrastructure Index (TII). Key areas for improvement include expanding the range and quality of end-to-end online public services, investing in innovative digital solutions, and enhancing user accessibility and experience

Summary_EN: Headline inflation averaged 0.68% YoY in Q4, slightly down from 0.73% YoY in Q3. It marked the lowest quarterly reading since Q1 2021.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Prices in the recreation and culture category remained the main driver of upward pressure on inflation in Q4, underpinned by strong demand associated with buoyant tourism activity. Meanwhile, the housing and utilities category remained the main drag on annual inflation in Q4 as rents continued to adjust downward. Among the main categories, three others made a negative contribution to annual inflation in Q4: food and beverages, furnishings and household equipment, and health.
  • Overall, Qatar's inflation eased to 1.1% last year, the lowest annual average since 2020. Regional inflation readings show Qatar had the third lowest inflation rate in the GCC in 2024 behind Oman and Bahrain, where price growth averaged 0.6% and 0.9%, respectively. In Saudi Arabia, the regionâ€™s largest economy, inflation averaged 1.7% in 2024, driven almost exclusively by upward pressure from housing rents. At 2.9%, Kuwait had the highest inflation rate in the region in 2024.
  • Consensus is for Qatarâ€™s inflation to average 1.6% this year and 1.7% in 2026, below the regional average of 2%. The January PMI survey show input costs continue to rise strongly, reflecting in large part, growing wage pressures. Meanwhile, output costs remain contained as firms absorb rising input costs rather than pass them on to consumers as they prioritise increasing sales volume.
  • Qatar Central Bank followed the US Federal Reserve in holding interest rates steady in January, which marked the first pause in the current cycle. In 2024, the US Fed delivered a cumulative 100bps of cuts. Meanwhile, the QCB cut rates by a total of 115bps (55bps in September, 30bps in November and 30bps in December). Currently, Qatarâ€™s deposit rate stands at 4.60%, the lending rate at 5.10% and the repo rate at 4.85%. The riyalâ€™s peg to the dollar is a constraint on how much Qatar Central Bank can deviate from the Fed and its likely moves will echo those of the US Fed in the coming months. The US Fed has signalled an extended pause, while financial markets point to a reduction in the fed funds rate of about 35bps through end-2025.

Summary_EN: • In 2023, Qatar ranked 83rd out of 145 countries in the Economic Complexity Index (ECI), highlighting the country's ongoing reliance on hydrocarbon exports and its limited economic diversification. The ECI, developed by Harvard Growth Lab, ranks countries based on their ability to produce and export a diverse and sophisticated mix of goods and services. Top-ranking countries in 2023 included Singapore, Switzerland, and Japan.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Qatarâ€™s ECI ranking in 2023 marks a decline of 21 positions compared to the previous year, reflecting challenges in transitioning toward a more complex and diversified economy. Despite sustained export volumes, the structure of Qatarâ€™s export basket remains concentrated in hydrocarbon-related products and moderately complex services, such as transport.
  • Total exports of goods and services reached QAR 468.5 billion in 2023. Of this, goods accounted for 76% and services 24%. Over the past decade, there has been a gradual shift toward services: the share of services exports rose from just 7.7% in 2013 to 24.1% in 2023. This trend was supported by growth in transport, tourism, and ICT, which hold promise for long-term productivity gains despite being less complex than advanced manufactured goods.
  • Qatar also lags behind its GCC peers in both export sophistication and diversification. In 2023, Qatar ranked lowest among GCC countries on the ECI: UAE 35, Bahrain 49, Saudi Arabia 60, Kuwait 64, Oman: 66.
  • Between 2008 and 2023, Qatar added only three new products to its export basket, compared to 40 for the UAE, 26 for Bahrain, 20 for Saudi Arabia, and 7 for Kuwait. This limited evolution suggests that Qatar's industrial base remains narrowly focused, and greater efforts are needed to expand into more complex and knowledge-intensive sectors.

Summary_EN:
Qatarâ€™s HS 2804 helium / rare gases exports are concentrated in six main destination markets: France, United States of America, Japan, United Arab Emirates, China, and Germany, with all other countries grouped as Others. Unlike LNG, which is mainly an energy-security export stream, helium and rare gases are smaller in value but strategically important because they support high-value sectors such as medical imaging, semiconductors, aerospace, advanced manufacturing, fiber optics, and scientific research.

The destination profile shows that Qatarâ€™s helium-related exports are linked to advanced industrial economies and technology supply chains. France and the United States represent major Western demand centers, while Japan, China, and Germany reflect industrial and high-technology demand. The UAE may also act as a regional destination or logistics hub. This makes the indicator useful not only for tracking export value, but also for monitoring Qatarâ€™s contribution to sensitive global supply chains.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
Qatarâ€™s helium / rare gases export profile under HS 2804 is strategically different from bulk energy commodities. Although the export value is much smaller than LNG or petroleum gases, the importance of helium lies in its scarcity, limited substitutability, and downstream industrial dependence. Helium is used in sectors where supply disruption can have consequences beyond trade value, especially in MRI systems, semiconductor production, aerospace, defense-related technologies, cryogenics, and scientific laboratories.

The monthly breakdown by country is valuable because helium-related shipments can be irregular. Movements may vary due to specialized container availability, contract delivery schedules, batch shipments, and destination-specific industrial demand. Therefore, month-to-month volatility should be interpreted carefully. A single monthly drop may reflect shipment timing rather than demand weakness, while repeated declines across multiple months may signal logistics constraints, production changes, or disruption in export flows.

The concentration of exports to France, the United States, Japan, UAE, China, and Germany indicates that Qatarâ€™s helium-related exports are connected to both Western and Asian advanced industrial systems. This gives Qatar strategic relevance beyond traditional hydrocarbon markets. In a disruption scenario, such as regional maritime instability, the impact may not be measured only by lost export value; it may also affect downstream industries that depend on reliable helium and rare gas supply.

From a route-risk perspective, helium and rare gases may have more logistics flexibility than LNG because they can be moved in specialized ISO containers and may use sea, land, or air depending on urgency, destination, and volume. However, Qatarâ€™s outbound export system still remains exposed to regional logistics conditions and maritime access.

Meanwhile, hydrogen and rare gases maintained their strong export momentum, posting a robust 15% quarter-on-quarter increase and 34% growth year-on-year, reflecting growing global demand for high-value, environmentally friendly products.

Summary_EN:
• Qatarâ€™s state budget revenues went up 5.4% both year-on-year and quarter-on-quarter

DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Qatarâ€™s state budget revenues reached QAR68.4bn in Q1 2023, up 5.4% both year-on-year and quarter-on-quarter.

Summary_EN: • The proportion of non-Qatari students who completed tertiary education, as a percentage of all post-secondary students, reached 55% in 2024, compared to 57% in 2023; a decline of 2 percentage points. The indicator also remained below the 2024 target of 60%.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• The indicator declined to 55% in 2024, compared to 57% in 2023, following 56% in 2022, reflecting continued limited fluctuation in tertiary completion rates among non-Qatari students in recent years.
  • The 2024 decline points to a lower proportion of non-Qatari students completing their university education relative to the previous year, while the indicator remained within a range close to its historical levels. It also underperformed the 2024 target of 60% by 5 percentage points.
  • This category shows a higher degree of volatility compared to Qatari students, which may be associated with demographic and educational factors, such as some students relocating to complete their studies abroad or year-to-year shifts in the composition of the resident student population. Despite the recorded decline, the indicator continues to reflect acceptable levels of tertiary completion among non-Qatari students.

Summary_EN:
• The education sectorâ€™s GDP increased by 1.9% in Q4 2025 compared to Q3, rising from QAR 4.49 bn to approximately QAR 4.58 bn.
  • The sector recorded 4.2% year-on-year growth in Q4 2025 compared to Q4 2024, increasing from approximately QAR 4.40 bn to QAR 4.58 bn.

  • On an annual basis, the sector grew by 1.7% in 2025 compared to 2024, with total GDP increasing from QAR 17.7 bn to approximately QAR 18.0 bn.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• The 1.9% quarter-on-quarter growth in Q4 2025 reflects continued recovery in sector activity and sustained momentum from Q3, with GDP increasing from QAR 4.49 bn to approximately QAR 4.58 bn. The 4.2% year-on-year growth compared to Q4 2024 (from approximately QAR 4.39 bn) indicates a relative acceleration in performance, reinforcing the sustained impact of recent investments and sector policies.
  • This performance aligns with the sectorâ€™s seasonal pattern, where Q4 maintains elevated levels of activity due to the stability of the academic year and full operational capacity, supporting continued momentum.
  • The sector demonstrated strong operational stability, maintaining output levels above QAR 4.5 bn, reflecting a smooth transition across activity cycles without structural slowdown.
  • On an annual basis, the 1.7% growth in 2025 compared to 2024 reflects continued gradual expansion, supported by government investments and infrastructure development, despite a relatively moderate pace compared to previous periods.
  • The education sector continues to play a central role in human capital development in Qatar, maintaining a stable contribution within the national economy and supporting Qatar National Vision 2030 toward a knowledge-based economy.

Despite the decline in land arrivals in September 2025, air arrivals rose 5.7%, reflecting continued strong global demand and minimal disruption from the 9 September attack.

  • Arrivals from European markets grew by around 9%, while non-Arab African markets saw a 31% increase. Visitor numbers from the Americas and Oceania remained stable y.o.y. Meanwhile, arrivals from China recorded notable growth of 24.1% y.o.y, despite security concerns.

  • The period typically marks the strongest quarter for non-hydrocarbon revenue collection. Non-hydrocarbon revenue collected in Q2 2024 represents 43.7% of the budget target (QAR 43 bn). Overall, the government targets a 21.2% share of non-hydrocarbon revenue in total revenue in its 2024 budget. Non-hydrocarbon revenue accounted for 16.9% of total government revenue in 2023. This compares to 9% in Kuwait, 28.1% in Oman and 37.8% in Saudi Arabia
DetailedAnalysis_EN: Non-hydrocarbon revenues continue to contribute less than a fifth of total government revenue (averaging 18.5% in 2015-23), leaving Qatarâ€™s budget among the least diversified in the GCC and most vulnerable to energy market trends. The share will likely decline in the medium-term given the projected rise in liquified natural gas export capacity though there is room to enact further revenue diversification measures, such as the introduction of the delayed VAT. It will be challenging to diversify revenue without taxing people more, either through direct or indirect measures. Qatar, alongside Kuwait, have yet to launch the tax, other GCC countries implemented the levy at 5% initially, with Saudi Arabia tripling the rate to 15% in mid-2020 and Bahrain doubling the rate to 10% in January 2022. Qatarâ€™s comparatively strong public finances mean thereâ€™s been less pressure to introduce the tax - it is on track to achieve the key 2030 fiscal sustainability targets including achieving a fiscal surplus of 5.5% of GDP, while maintaining credit ratings at the current AA/Aa2 level

Summary_EN:
• Qatari Medical graduates are vital for public health, economic impact and national development of human capital goals (NDS3). With a current output of 24 and a target of 150 graduates by 2030 requiring significant annual increases, strategic planning, investment in training capacity and accurate reporting of all medical graduates.
  • Currently, the number of graduates is being reported from Qatar University, MOPH, MOEHE and NPC will need to capture proper data including Weill Cornell Qatar and Qatari students graduating from international medical schools i.e. Bahrain, etc. Accurate data reporting of all medical graduates is essential for effective healthcare planning and resource allocation, as underestimating the workforce can cause disparities and suboptimal policy decisions like building a healthcare workforce pipeline.
  • Challenges include raising awareness of healthcare careers, ensuring adequate academic preparation, addressing financial barriers, and providing support systems to foster a diverse and prepared pool of future medical doctors.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Qatari medical graduates are critical for Qatarâ€™s healthcare system and overall economic stability providing a national workforce rooted in community. Qatari doctors play an essential role in maintaining positive social and public health outcomes, enhancing productivity, and serving as role models for future Qatari medical students.

  • Currently, the medical graduate output stands at 24, with a target of 150 graduates by 2030. Achieving this goal is ambitious but potentially feasible with strategic planning and implementation. To meet the target, the annual number of graduates would need to increase significantly, requiring a commitment to expanding training capacity. Specifically, moving from 24 to 150 in about seven years necessitates an average increase of approximately 18 graduates per year. However, several challenges must be addressed to create a sustainable pipeline of students entering the healthcare field:

    - MOPH, MOEHE and NPC need to work together towards a centralized and strategic approach to awareness of career opportunities in healthcare for students at all levels especially primary education level. 
    - Students must have access to quality pre-medical education that prepares them for the rigorous demands of medical training. 
    - Enhancing STEM education at earlier levels can help ensure that prospective students are adequately prepared.

  • Moreover, if Qatar only reports graduates from one institution and fails to capture those from other sources, the implications could be significant. This oversight can lead to an underestimation of the healthcare workforce, affecting policy formulation and funding decisions. It may lead to disparities in healthcare access and quality, diminish the perceived value of contributions from unreported institutions, and hinder effective workforce planning.
  • The target of 150 medical graduates by 2030 is challenging, it is achievable through concerted efforts in addressing the pipeline challenges, strategic planning, resource allocation, and collaboration among stakeholders in the education and healthcare sectors. Comprehensive data collection and accurate reporting of medical graduates are essential for informed decision-making, effective healthcare delivery, and the economic well-being of the population.

Summary_EN: With the Strait of Hormuz closed, Qatarâ€™s export revenue exposure becomes immediate and material. Qatarâ€™s key export commodities â€” especially LNG/petroleum gases, condensate, refined petroleum products, fertilizers, ammonia, sulphur, polymers, and aluminium â€” are heavily dependent on maritime routes. The closure directly disrupts Qatarâ€™s ability to move high-value commodities to global markets, creating risks of delayed shipments, deferred revenues, higher freight and insurance costs, contract delivery pressure, and possible production or storage constraints.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz represents a direct shock to Qatarâ€™s export system because the countryâ€™s highest-value export categories are predominantly sea-based. LNG and petroleum gases are the most exposed, as they rely on specialized carriers and established maritime routes to reach major Asian and European buyers. With the Strait closed, Qatarâ€™s ability to convert LNG production into export revenue is constrained, even if global LNG prices rise due to supply fears.

The impact extends beyond LNG. Condensate, crude-related exports, refined fuels, fertilizers, ammonia, sulphur, polymers, and aluminium are also exposed because they rely on bulk, tanker, or containerized maritime movement. Fertilizers and ammonia are especially important because they connect Qatarâ€™s gas-based industrial sector to global agricultural input and food-security supply chains. Disruption to these exports affects both Qatarâ€™s industrial revenues and importing countriesâ€™ access to key production inputs.

From a revenue perspective, the main issue is not only price volatility, but export continuity. Higher global prices may increase the value of available cargoes, but if shipments cannot move, revenue realization is delayed or reduced. The closure also increases commercial pressure through possible contract penalties, buyer uncertainty, demurrage, rerouting constraints, insurance premiums, and operational pressure on storage and production planning.

The airport welcomed over 13.7 million passengers, reflecting a 7.9% growth compared to the same period in the previous year. Additionally, 670,643 tons of cargo were handled, marking a 13.5% increase compared to Q3-2023, with cargo volumes remaining stable throughout the quarter. In a strategic move, the airport announced a partnership with Siemens in July 2024 to enhance central cooling infrastructure, aiming to optimize energy consumption and support the airportâ€™s sustainable growth plans.

Summary_EN:
• Between Q3 2022 and Q4 2022, the balance of goods declined by 21.1% owning to a large decline in goods exports due to lower energy prices

  • Comparing Q4 2021 and Q4 2022, the balance of goods increased by 10.7%
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Between Q3 2022 and Q4 2022, the balance of goods declined by 21.1% owning to a large decline in goods exports due to lower energy prices (Source: https://tradingeconomics.com/commodity/natural-gas). Comparing Q4 2021 and Q4 2022, the balance of goods increased by 10.7% given that by end of 2022, the Covid-19 emergency had waned and re-opening spurred additional demand for goods

  • In Q4 2022 the balance of services narrowed significantly compared to Q3 2022 due to the World Cup which recorded a jump on travel exports by 123.2%. Comparing to the same quarter in 2021, a similar picture is observed with travel exports jumping by 135.7%, increasing overall services exports by 132.6%. Q4 2022 is an aberration to a general trend of a rather deep services deficit which requires a surplus in oil and natural gas exports to sustain national income

  • The overall trade balance dropped by 15.8% between Q3 and Q4 2022, but when measured between Q4 2021 and Q4 2022, it improved by 38.7%. The same reasons delineated previously in the text drove also the overall trade balance

Summary_EN:
• Real GDP grew by 6.1% YoY in Q4 2024. The non-hydrocarbon GDP registered 6.1% YoY growth, lifting the headline GDP by 3.9ppt. Meanwhile, the hydrocarbon GDP grew by 6.2% YoY, adding 2.2ppt to headline GDP growth.
  • Taken together, real GDP grew by 2.4% YoY in 2024. This is 0.8ppt higher than GDP growth in 2023.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Taken together, real GDP grew by 2.4% YoY in 2024. This is 0.8ppt higher than GDP growth in 2023.
  • Non-hydrocarbon sectors drove growth during 2024, expanding 3.4% YoY, above the 2.1% pace in 2023 and nearer the 4% annual expansion targeted in Qatarâ€™s Third National Development Strategy.
  • Expansion in 2024 reflected strong performance in real estate activities, construction, wholesale and retail trade and education sectors. Manufacturing made a negative contribution to growth with growth declining by 2.2% in 2024. This is the first year since 2020 that Qatari manufacturing output has declined.
  • Meanwhile, the hydrocarbon sector grew by 0.6% YoY in 2024, contrasting the decline in industrial production. The rate of expansion was similar to 2023 and marked the third positive annual performance since 2012.
  • During Q4 specifically, construction and financial services made the largest positive contribution to annual growth, extending the trends from Q3.
  • Consensus is for Qatarâ€™ economic growth to be steady at 2.6% this year, with both the energy and non-energy sectors contributing positively to growth. The projection lies below the regional average of 3.7%. Consensus then sees GDP growth gaining pace to 5.3% in 2026, as the additional LNG capacity starts up, above the GCC average of 4.1%.

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and related conflict disruption has shifted Qatarâ€™s LNG situation from a shipping-route issue into a contractual supply disruption. QatarEnergy has already declared force majeure on some affected LNG contracts, meaning certain delivery obligations cannot be fulfilled under normal contractual terms due to events outside the supplierâ€™s control.

Strait of Hormuz disruption is expected to materially slow global trade growth in 2026. After recovering strongly from a contraction in 2023, global merchandise trade growth is estimated to reach 4.7% in 2025, but is then forecast to fall sharply to a range of 1.5% to 2.5% in 2026.

The Hormuz disruption is not being read as a narrow regional shipping issue; it is being treated as a global trade shock. The expected slowdown reflects the importance of Hormuz as a critical corridor for energy and commodity flows. Disruption at this chokepoint raises transport risk, increases energy and insurance costs, and weakens trade momentum across multiple regions and sectors.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
The Strait of Hormuz disruption represents a material shock to global trade. After recovering from contraction in 2023, merchandise trade growth strengthened to an estimated 4.7% in 2025, indicating renewed momentum in global goods flows. That momentum is now expected to weaken sharply in 2026, with growth forecast to fall to between 1.5% and 2.5%. This signals a clear deterioration in the external trade environment within a short period.

The expected slowdown reflects the strategic importance of Hormuz as a key corridor for global energy and commodity movements. Disruption at this chokepoint increases shipping risk, raises insurance and transport costs, and adds uncertainty to delivery timelines and input pricing. The consequence is broader than the immediate region: trade becomes more costly, less predictable, and less efficient across global supply chains. Overall, the chart points to weaker trade expansion, tighter operating conditions for trade-dependent sectors, and rising downside risk to global economic activity in 2026.

Summary_EN: • Real GDP grew by 6.1% YoY in Q4 2024. The non-hydrocarbon GDP registered 6.1% YoY growth, lifting the headline GDP by 3.9ppt. Meanwhile, the hydrocarbon GDP grew by 6.2% YoY, adding 2.2ppt to headline GDP growth.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Taken together, real GDP grew by 2.4% YoY in 2024. This is 0.8ppt higher than GDP growth in 2023.
  • Non-hydrocarbon sectors drove growth during 2024, expanding 3.4% YoY, above the 2.1% pace in 2023 and nearer the 4% annual expansion targeted in Qatarâ€™s Third National Development Strategy.
  • Expansion in 2024 reflected strong performance in real estate activities, construction, wholesale and retail trade and education sectors. Manufacturing made a negative contribution to growth with growth declining by 2.2% in 2024. This is the first year since 2020 that Qatari manufacturing output has declined.
  • Meanwhile, the hydrocarbon sector grew by 0.6% YoY in 2024, contrasting the decline in industrial production. The rate of expansion was similar to 2023 and marked the third positive annual performance since 2012.
  • During Q4 specifically, construction and financial services made the largest positive contribution to annual growth, extending the trends from Q3.
  • Consensus is for Qatarâ€™ economic growth to be steady at 2.6% this year, with both the energy and non-energy sectors contributing positively to growth. The projection lies below the regional average of 3.7%. Consensus then sees GDP growth gaining pace to 5.3% in 2026, as the additional LNG capacity starts up, above the GCC average of 4.1%.

Summary_EN: • Investment into the sector declined by 13% on a QoQ basis in Q4 2025, while registering a strong annual growth of 58%. When assessed against the strategic plan targets, the industrial investment indicator achieved only 49% of the planned level for Q4 2025.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Despite the relatively weak aggregate performance, basic industries continued to exhibit investment resilience, with the launch of 18 new factories. Investment activity was concentrated in chemical industries, particularly fertilizer manufacturing, where 2 new facilities were commissioned, including Gulf Formaldehyde Company, in addition to other chemical production plants such as Sika Factory.

  • The fabricated metals sector recorded notable investment inflows totaling QAR 51 million, reflected in the establishment of 2 new plants specializing in fabricated metal equipment. At the same time, the food manufacturing sector sustained its investment momentum, with 3 new factories commencing operations during Q4 2025, supported by investments amounting to QAR 23 million.

  • The plastics manufacturing sector demonstrated continued investment activity, with QAR 24 million invested through the opening of 3 new production facilities over the same period.

Summary_EN: Total exports reached QAR 116.9 bn in Q2-2024, down by 2.4% compared to last quarter but up 6.1%, compared to a year ago.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Total exports reached QAR 116.9 bn in Q2-2024, down by 2.4% compared to last quarter but up 6.1%, compared to a year ago. Exports of goods declined by 3% compared to last quarter and by 0.4% compared to a year ago. Gas and crude oil exports saw declines both YoY and QoQ bases, while non-crude oil saw some increase by 7.1% in Q2-2024 compared to last quarter. The declines were in spite of Brent oil increases compared both to last quarter and last year, which could indicate either lower production or lower demand. Re-exports did not show any significant pattern of change remaining in the region of QAR 3-3.5 bn over the last several quarters. Exports of other goods represent 11.3% of total goods exports in Q2-2024 and exhibit a correlation of around 80% with oil-related exports, indicating that these exports are also dependent on oil-related inputs
  • Services exports saw an impressive YoY increase in Q2-2024 by 28.3% but slightly lower compared to last quarter by 0.7%. YoY increases on services exports were evidenced in all sub-accounts, travel, transportation and other exports. Total visitorsâ€™ numbers saw an increase of 13.5% compared to a year ago and a decrease of 37.8% compared to last quarter, reaching 1 million visitors in Q2-2024. After a rather strong Q1-2024, air arrivals dropped by 24% compared to last quarter but still up by 11.2% compared to a year ago, reaching 585,655 visitors. Land arrivals followed a similar pattern, after a particular strong Q1-2024, with decline by 34.4% in Q2-2024 but up 20.2% compared to a year ago, reaching 417,291 visitors. Sea arrivals followed the seasonal pattern of decreased Q2 arrivals
  • As the US economy is expected to do a soft landing after inflation has been declining without major recessionary episodes, Brent oil prices are expected to remain within the USD 82-84 per barrel range. According to the US Energy Information Administration, they expect the Brent crude oil spot price to average USD 82 per barrel in Q4-2024 and average USD 84 per barrel in 2025, indicating a rather flattish outlook for Qatarâ€™s exports given current production

Summary_EN: In 2022, Qatar ranked 84th out of 145 in the Economic Complexity Index, reflecting limited diversification and continued reliance on hydrocarbon exports
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
Qatar ranked 84th out of 145 countries in the 2022 Economic Complexity Index (ECI), a decline of 11 positions from 2021. The countryâ€™s ECI remains below the level expected for its income, reflecting limited economic diversification and continued reliance on hydrocarbon exports. Exports have remained broadly stable, driven primarily by products of moderate complexity, particularly hydrocarbon-related goods and transport services.

The ECI, developed by Harvard University, ranks countries based on their capacity to produce and export a diverse and sophisticated mix of goods and services. In 2022, the highest-ranking economies were Japan, South Korea, and Switzerland. Between 2007 and 2022, Qatar added four new products to its export basket, compared to 10 products for Saudi Arabia (ranked 44th in 2022), 15 for the United Arab Emirates (ranked 62nd in 2022), and three for Kuwait (ranked 121st in 2022).

DetailedAnalysis_EN:
•  The slight decline in the education sectorâ€™s GDP during Q2 2025 indicates that the sector has entered a stabilization phase following the significant expansion witnessed over the past two years. The modest decrease of 0.22% compared to Q2 2024 shows that activity levels remain close to their peak, reflecting the continued positive impact of major educational investments carried out in 2023 and 2024.
  • The quarter-on-quarter decline of 1.07% compared to Q1 2025 is attributed to the typical seasonal factors affecting the education sector. Q2 coincides with the end of the academic year and the summer break, a period that normally sees reduced academic activity and lower institutional spending, resulting in a temporary drop in output.
  • This seasonal decrease represents a natural correction in the sectorâ€™s annual performance cycle rather than a structural slowdown in growth. It reflects a transitional phase between peak educational activity and preparation for the new academic year. Maintaining output levels above QAR 4.4 bn in Q2 demonstrates the sectorâ€™s ability to preserve its operational gains without any fundamental decline.
  • The education sector remains one of the key drivers of human development in Qatar, maintaining its vital role within the national economy. This stable performance aligns with ongoing government policies aimed at enhancing the educational infrastructure, improving the efficiency of schools and universities, and implementing initiatives to develop national talents. Collectively, these efforts strengthen the sectorâ€™s contribution to achieving the goals of Qatar National Vision 2030.

Summary_EN: Qatar ranked 9th out of 69 economies in the 2025 IMD World Competitiveness Index, continuing a steady upward trajectory from 17th in 2021. This performance reflects sustained improvements in key dimensions of national competitiveness.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Qatar has achieved a significant milestone, advancing to ninth place in the 2025 IMD World Competitiveness Ranking, marking its first entry into the top 10 most competitive economies globally. This improvement, up from 11th in the previous year, reflects continued momentum across multiple dimensions of competitiveness, most notably in Business Efficiency (ranked fifth), while maintaining strong positions in both Government Efficiency and Economic Performance (ranked seventh in each).
  • Qatarâ€™s performance was further bolstered by specific sub-indicators. The country achieved the second-lowest unemployment rate globally. However, this outcome is influenced by the structure of the labor market, where the majority of the workforce consists of expatriates whose legal residence is contingent upon employment. Qatar also retained high rankings in tax policy (second) and homicide rate (first), underscoring a favorable fiscal and security environment.
  • Despite these strengths, several structural challenges remain. Qatar ranked 45th in Scientific Infrastructure, reflecting limited investment in research and development and a relatively low volume of patent activity. Environmental indicators also point to areas of concern, with the country ranking 69th in exposure to particulate pollution and 65th in the share of renewable energy in total consumption. In the education sector, Qatar lags behind peer economies, ranking 65th in public education expenditure, 52nd in higher education attainment, and 42nd in the university education index. These findings highlight the need for continued reforms to strengthen innovation, sustainability, and human capital, key priorities under the Third National Development Strategy and essential to achieving the goals of Qatar National Vision 2030.

Expenditure of QR 48.3 billion in Q1 2026 is not abnormally high â€” it broadly reflects normal Q1 levels. The deficit is a revenue shortfall, not an expenditure overshoot. Salaries and wages plus current expenditure together form a structurally fixed base. Major Capex is the only adjustable element, but even eliminating it entirely would not close a QR 10.3 billion gap driven by a revenue collapse.

  • The performance of Qatarâ€™s manufacturing sector continues to be affected by several structural challenges, including delays in implementing the industrial strategy, high production costs, slow adoption of Fourth Industrial Revolution technologies, weak integration into global supply chains, and procedural complexities compared to neighboring Gulf countries.
  • Qatarâ€™s private sector exports witnessed notable growth in Q4-2024, reaching QAR 3.4 bn through the general model, an increase of 66% compared to QAR 2.1 bn in Q4-2023. This rise aligns with Qatarâ€™s ongoing efforts to diversify its economy and reduce reliance on hydrocarbons.
  • The petrochemical segment of Industries Qatar maintained its profit levels compared to the previous year, as a 10% increase in sales volume offset the pressure of narrowing margins and global market volatility, especially in products like polyethylene and methanol.
  • The iron and steel segment of Industries Qatar experienced a decline in revenues due to falling global demand and lower selling prices in 2024. However, the restart of the Direct Reduction Unit (DR-1) at Qatar Steel in Q4 contributed to increased productivity during the last quarter of the year.
  • Qatarâ€™s manufacturing sector is largely based on petrochemicals, fertilizers, and metals. The country remains classified as an industrial economy reliant on primary commodities and sectors that were heavily impacted by global price fluctuations in 2024. This stands in contrast to peers like Saudi Arabia and the UAE, whose industries have diversified into more resilient sectors such as machinery, pharmaceuticals, and food industries.
  • Qatarâ€™s comprehensive industrial strategy was only launched at the end of 2024, and its impact during the year was limited, restricted to a few quick wins.

• The Global Cybersecurity Index (GCI), issued by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), provides insights into a country's cybersecurity readiness and capabilities. It evaluates various factors related to cybersecurity, including legal frameworks, technical measures, organizational structures, capacity building, and cooperative measures.
  • Qatar GCI rank declined from 17 in 2018 to 27 in 2020 but is ranked 5th regionally.
  • KSA, UAE, Oman, and Egypt are regional countries ranked higher than Qatar, with Qatar scoring 94.5%, trailing behind KSA (99.54%), UAE (98.06%), and Oman (96.04%), while Egypt scored slightly lower than Qatar at 95.48%. This indicates that despite Qatar's commendable commitment, evident in its high overall score, its lower ranking can be primarily attributed to weaknesses in the technical measures pillar, such as the need to enhance the capabilities of Computer Incident Response Teams (CIRT) and sector-specific agencies.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Qatar has taken significant steps to improve its cybersecurity infrastructure. The establishment of the National Cybersecurity Agency (NCSA) in March 2021 introduced a comprehensive cybersecurity framework for both public and private sectors.
  • The NCSA's inclusive strategy, covering public, and private organizations, has expanded cybersecurity capabilities across diverse sectors. Noteworthy efforts include targeted cybersecurity awareness campaigns in public schools and extensive training for government employees.
  • As the 5th edition of the Global Cybersecurity Index (GCI) approaches, Qatar's significant progress in committing to cybersecurity practices positions the nation optimistically for an improved ranking in the upcoming report.

DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Prices in the recreation and culture category remained the main driver of upward pressure on inflation in Q4, underpinned by strong demand associated with buoyant tourism activity. Meanwhile, the housing and utilities category remained the main drag on annual inflation in Q4 as rents continued to adjust downward. Among the main categories, three others made a negative contribution to annual inflation in Q4: food and beverages, furnishings and household equipment, and health

  • Overall, Qatar's inflation eased to 1.1% last year, the lowest annual average since 2020. Regional inflation readings show Qatar had the third lowest inflation rate in the GCC in 2024 behind Oman and Bahrain, where price growth averaged 0.6% and 0.9%, respectively. In Saudi Arabia, the regionâ€™s largest economy, inflation averaged 1.7% in 2024, driven almost exclusively by upward pressure from housing rents. At 2.9%, Kuwait had the highest inflation rate in the region in 2024

  • Consensus is for Qatarâ€™s inflation to average 1.6% this year and 1.7% in 2026, below the regional average of 2%. The January PMI survey show input costs continue to rise strongly, reflecting in large part, growing wage pressures. Meanwhile, output costs remain contained as firms absorb rising input costs rather than pass them on to consumers as they prioritise increasing sales volume

  • Qatar Central Bank followed the US Federal Reserve in holding interest rates steady in January, which marked the first pause in the current cycle. In 2024, the US Fed delivered a cumulative 100bps of cuts. Meanwhile, the QCB cut rates by a total of 115bps (55bps in September, 30bps in November and 30bps in December). Currently, Qatarâ€™s deposit rate stands at 4.60%, the lending rate at 5.10% and the repo rate at 4.85%. The riyalâ€™s peg to the dollar is a constraint on how much Qatar Central Bank can deviate from the Fed and its likely moves will echo those of the US Fed in the coming months. The US Fed has signalled an extended pause, while financial markets point to a reduction in the fed funds rate of about 35bps through end-2025

  • In the medium-term, government revenue will benefit from the projected rise in liquified natural gas export capacity as well as future revenue diversification measures, such as the introduction of VAT at an unspecified time.

Summary_EN: Qatar's total public debt has been on a disciplined downward path since its Q1 2025 peak of QR 338.6 billion, driven by consistent quarterly redemptions. The external-domestic split is broadly balanced at 51%/49%, with the external share improving. This reflects sound liability management. However, the Q1 2026 deficit of QR 10.3 billion introduces a new risk: if revenues remain depressed and deficits continue at this scale, the State will need to issue new debt to finance them â€” reversing the deleveraging trend achieved over the past year.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
Public debt reached its highest level in the displayed period at QAR 338.6bn in Q1 2025, before declining by QAR 7.4bn in Q2 and a further QAR 2.3bn in Q3. The Q3 reduction was modest, but it extended the downward movement in the overall debt stock.

The earlier increase in debt was associated with external financing activity, including the USD 2.5bn green bond issued in Q2 2024 and the USD 3.0bn bond issued in February 2025. Subsequent repayments and maturities appear to have reduced the external debt component during 2025.

External debt remains the larger share of total public debt, while domestic debt has remained comparatively stable across the period. This suggests that the reduction achieved during 2025 was concentrated in the external borrowing portfolio rather than domestic financing.

The QAR 10.3bn Q1 2026 fiscal deficit creates a potential financing requirement. If the full deficit were financed through net new debt, with no offsetting redemptions or alternative funding sources, the outstanding debt stock could rise to approximately QAR 339.2bn based on the Q3 2025 debt level. This would exceed the Q1 2025 peak.

The actual outcome will depend on the governmentâ€™s financing mix, redemption schedule, cash reserves, oil and gas revenue performance, expenditure controls, and the timing of capital projects. The principal risk is not the deficit itself, but the extent to which it results in additional borrowing after repayments are considered.

  • The declines in natural gas prices were a corrective movement following record highs during 2022. Geopolitical tensions between Russia and Ukraine and storage issues had contributed to the previous price surge.

• Export time refers to the average time required to process and dispatch shipments via air, sea, and land. It involves several steps, including document preparation by the private sector and clearance agencies, customs clearance and inspections carried out by the Customs Authority and other government entities, inland transport managed by logistics providers, and port/airport handling by operators like Mwani Qatar and Hamad International Airport

  • In Q2-2024, the Customs Authority successfully reduced the export time by 25% compared to Q1-2024, with the improvements primarily benefiting both restricted and unrestricted goods
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• The reduction in export time is due to improvements in customs clearance procedures, which constitute a significant portion of the overall export time. Initiatives such as the GCC Agreement on National Products, mobile inspections for restricted goods, and the implementation of the approved economic operators list have streamlined the export process, enabling faster procedures and reducing delays

  • However, other aspects of the export process, such as document preparation, inland transport, and terminal handling, currently lack sufficient data to be fully integrated into the export time calculations. The Ministry of Transport is working on developing data for these components, and once available, they will be incorporated into the overall calculation to provide a more comprehensive analysis of export efficiency

This expansion was largely driven by sustained production activity across several key subsectors. The beverages industry led quarterly growth with a 4.4% increase, supported by rising domestic demand. The rubber and plastics products sector followed with a 3% increase, while refined petroleum products posted a 2.2% increase.
  • The food production sector recorded a 10% year-on-year increase in Q2-2025, driven by a 27% annual rise in dairy production. This performance reflects the success of government policies aimed at strengthening the role of the private sector.
  • Conversely, certain segments of the manufacturing sector faced notable headwinds, particularly those linked to infrastructure and construction, such as cement industry which continued to exert downward pressure on performance. The chemicals and petrochemicals industries were particularly affected, recording a 1.1% contraction quarter-on-quarter and a 5% decline year-on-year. These results were driven by lower sales prices and weakening external demand, adversely impacting the revenues of several firms during Q2-2025.

DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Revenue collected in Q3 represents 25.4% of the central government's budget estimate for the year (QAR 202bn). It leaves the total revenue collected year-to-date (Q1-Q3) at 81.5% of the 2024 budget estimate. Hydrocarbon revenue collected in Q1-Q3 represents 82.2% of the budget target (QAR 159bn), while non-hydrocarbon revenue represents 78.7% of the budget target (QAR 43bn) The government revenue for 2023 was QAR 254bn, which was above the 5-year pre-pandemic average of QAR 202.5bn.

  • Brent oil price averaged US$80.1pb in the year to end-November, compared to the US$60pb assumed in the 2024 budget, while natural gas prices appear to have stabilised. In the medium-term, government revenue will benefit from the projected rise in liquified natural gas export capacity as well as further revenue diversification measures. The 2025 budget extends support for the economy, with total expenditures set at QAR 210.2bn and total revenues estimated at QAR 197bn, resulting in a QAR 13.2bn budget deficit. Key allocations include QAR 19.4bn for education to construct new schools and facilities, and QAR 22bn for health to expand hospitals and upgrade services.

  • QIC reported gross written premiums of QAR 7.9 bn in Q3 2025, reflecting a 9% YoY increase from Q3 2024. This increase is due to QIC continuing to benefit from strong economic conditions in its core markets due to its strategic shift toward profitable regions. This strategic shift can be seen in QICâ€™s share of GWPs from domestic and MENA operations, which increased from 54% to 60% YoY, while international business reduced from 46% to 40% of GWPs.

    Regarding Q3 2025, the decline reported by several companies is mainly due to changes in underwriting strategies and the non-renewal of key policies:

  • Qatar General Insurance & Reinsurance Co: Premiums fell due to stopping renewal of loss-making policies, such as vehicle and medical insurance, and the expiry of a major project policy issued last year worth QAR 120 million. Competition and reduced reliance on brokers also contributed.
  • QIIC: The decline in motor premiums resulted from postponing renewal of a large policy at the clientâ€™s request, while the decrease in health insurance came from applying a selective underwriting approach to reduce risk.
  • General Takaful: The drop was mainly in vehicle insurance due to reduced underwriting participations, particularly indirect contributions from brokers. Medical premiums also decreased due to the non-renewal of some policies previously sourced from other insurers.

Summary_EN:

Hydrocarbon revenue collected in H1 represents 55.6% of the budget target (QAR 159 bn), while non-hydrocarbon revenue represents 57.9% of the budget target (QAR 43 bn) The government revenue for 2023 was QAR 254 bn, which was above the 5-year pre-pandemic average of QAR 202.5 bn
DetailedAnalysis_EN: Government revenue looks on track to surpass budget estimates this year as the oil price has averaged US$82.5 pb year-to-date, compared to the US$ 60 pb assumed in the bill and natural gas prices appear to have stabilised. The comparatively strong outlook for public finances means that Qatar should be relatively unconstrained in supporting growth and will continue to allocate budgets boosting economic contribution of non-energy sectors

DetailedAnalysis_EN: The drivers of inflation shifted during the quarter. Meanwhile, the drag on annual inflation from the housing and utilities category deepened in Q1, with prices falling 4.52% YoY, the most since Q3 2021. The Discounted Goods Initiative launched by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry ahead of Ramadan will have likely contributed to this fall. Among the main categories, three others made a negative contribution to annual inflation in Q1: furnishings and household equipment, transport and restaurants and hotels. Conversely, communication prices were the main driver of upward pressure on inflation in Q1, alongside prices of miscellaneous goods and services.

Summary_EN: • Qatar's ranking in the Network Readiness Index (NRI) improved significantly from 46th in 2023 to 38th in 2024, with a score of 57.31. However, Qatar's performance is below the trend line when considering its GDP per capita compared to other high-income countries. The UAE ranked 27th, and Saudi Arabia ranked 37th, both outperforming Qatar regionally.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• In 2024, Qatar demonstrated strong performance across several sub-indicators within the NRI, reflecting progress in adopting advanced networks and investing in emerging technologies. Its strengths included leading the globe in 3G network coverage and internet access in schools, both ranked 1st worldwide. Qatar also performed exceptionally well in the use of virtual social networks, achieving 4th place globally, and demonstrated robust ICT skills within its education system, ranked 8th
  • Occupying the 38th spot globally, Qatar showcases robust digital advancement, excelling in the Access (34th) and Future Technologies (13th) dimensions. Notably, it ranks 8th in having digitally ready individuals. Qatar also achieves commendable results in sustained Investment (17th) and Adoption (19th) of emerging technologies, underpinned by a strong performance in Government promotion of investment in emerging technologies (8th)
  • Despite these achievements, challenges remain, particularly in areas like AI scientific contributions, where Qatar ranked 100th globally, and privacy protection in legal content, which was ranked 90th. Additionally, the country struggled with e-participation, ranking 89th, and faced ongoing difficulties in improving digital content, building internet subscription, and contributing effectively to SDGs
  • To keep improving, Qatar should focus on strengthening its regulatory and legal frameworks, especially in privacy protection and e-participation. It also needs to address weaknesses in SDG contributions and digital content. Aligning its NRI performance with its GDP per capita will help position Qatar more competitively on the global stage

Summary_EN: In Q4 2025, Qatar exported around QAR 2.30 billion of fertilizer and ammonia products, led mainly by nitrogenous fertilizers. The export base was concentrated in Singapore, the United States, Switzerland, and Japan, demonstrating strong pre-2026 demand from major trading hubs and end markets. This quarter provides an important baseline: Qatar entered 2026 with active, high-value fertilizer and ammonia export flows, making any subsequent Strait of Hormuz disruption a direct shock to an already significant export network.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
In Q4 2025, Qatarâ€™s fertilizer and ammonia exports reached approximately QAR 2.30 billion, showing a strong export position immediately before the 2026 disruption period. Export value was relatively steady across the quarter, with October at QAR 852.74 million, November at QAR 728.23 million, and December at QAR 714.10 million. This indicates that Qatar entered 2026 with an already active and sizeable export base for fertilizer and ammonia products.

The quarter was highly concentrated in a small number of destination markets. Singapore was the largest destination, receiving around QAR 737.81 million, followed closely by the United States of America at QAR 727.88 million. Switzerland ranked third with QAR 367.70 million, followed by Japan at QAR 286.70 million. Smaller but still relevant flows went to the UAE, Australia, and India. This shows that Qatarâ€™s export network was already anchored around major trading hubs and strategic end markets before the conflict-related disruption.

From a product perspective, Q4 2025 was overwhelmingly driven by HS 3102 â€” nitrogenous mineral or chemical fertilizers, which accounted for approximately QAR 2.05 billion, or around 89% of the quarterâ€™s total. HS 2814 â€” ammonia accounted for approximately QAR 242.01 million, or around 11%. This reinforces that the main exposure was fertilizer-led, while ammonia remained a strategically important supporting export stream.

Summary_EN:

It evaluates various factors related to cybersecurity, including legal frameworks, technical measures, organizational structures, capacity building, and cooperative measures

  • Qatar GCI rank declined from 17 in 2018 to 27 in 2020, but is ranked 5th regionally

  • KSA, UAE, Oman, and Egypt are regional countries ranked higher than Qatar, with Qatar scoring 94.5%, trailing behind KSA (99.54%), UAE (98.06%), and Oman (96.04%), while Egypt scored slightly lower than Qatar at 95.48%. This indicates that despite Qatar's commendable commitment, evident in its high overall score, its lower ranking can be primarily attributed to weaknesses in the technical measures pillar, such as the need to enhance the capabilities of Computer Incident Response Teams (CIRT) and sector-specific agencies
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Qatar has taken significant steps to improve its cybersecurity infrastructure. The establishment of the National Cybersecurity Agency (NCSA) in March 2021 introduced a comprehensive cybersecurity framework for both public and private sectors.

  • The NCSA's inclusive strategy, covering public, and private organizations, has expanded cybersecurity capabilities across diverse sectors. Noteworthy efforts include targeted cybersecurity awareness campaigns in public schools and extensive training for government employees.

  • As the 5th edition of the Global Cybersecurity Index (GCI) approaches, Qatar's significant progress in committing to cybersecurity practices positions the nation optimistically for an improved ranking in the upcoming report

Summary_EN: • In 2026, Qatar ranked 11th out of 70 economies in the IMD World Competitiveness Yearbook, down two places from its 9th position in 2025. Despite this decline, Qatar remained among the top 15 economies globally, underscoring its continued strong competitiveness position.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Qatar continued to perform strongly across several key indicators. It ranked second globally in Employment, Tax Policy, Labor Market, Basic Infrastructure and Attitudes & Values. The country was also among the global top 5 in GDP per capita on a purchasing-power basis, low inflation, efficient management of public finances and energy infrastructure. Surveyed business leaders identified reliable infrastructure and stable, predictable policy as Qatarâ€™s main attractiveness factors.
  • The decline in Qatarâ€™s overall ranking was mainly driven by weaker performance in 2 of the 4 pillars. Economic Performance fell from 7th to 13th, while Business Efficiency declined from 5th to 10th. In contrast, Government Efficiency remained stable at 7th, and Infrastructure improved from 30th to 27th.
  • The largest downward contribution came from international trade, where Qatarâ€™s ranking fell by 18 places to 56th. This reflected lower exports of commercial services, alongside a narrower current-account surplus. The Domestic Economy ranking also declined from 12th to 25th. These developments point to a softer year for hydrocarbon-linked output and external balances, rather than a structural weakening of the economy.
  • However, some structural challenges remain. Qatar ranked 44th in Scientific Infrastructure and 37th in Health & Environment, reflecting relatively low research and development activity, modest patent performance, and a limited renewable-energy share. Other areas requiring attention include high-tech and ICT-service exports, inbound foreign investment and export concentration. Addressing these gaps would support the diversification objectives of the Third National Development Strategy (NDS3) and Qatar National Vision 2030.

Summary_EN:
• Qatar entered the 2026 conflict period with LNG export values already below the previous yearâ€™s level. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz now poses a direct threat to a strategically vital export system
  • According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), more than 110 bcm of LNG transited through the Strait in 2025, including around 93% of Qatarâ€™s LNG exports, representing nearly one-fifth of global LNG trade.
  • The exposure is particularly concentrated in Asia, with the IEA estimating that nearly 90% of LNG volumes transiting the Strait are destined for Asian markets, placing China, India, South Korea, Japan, and Pakistan among the most vulnerable importers.
  • Following QatarEnergyâ€™s force majeure declaration, the disruption shifted from a shipping issue to a contractual supply crisis affecting delivery reliability and buyer confidence. As importers seek alternative LNG suppliers, competition for replacement cargoes is intensifying, placing additional upward pressure on global gas prices.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• The Strait of Hormuz crisis represents a multi-layered shock to Qatarâ€™s export economy, with LNG exports standing at the forefront as the countryâ€™s most visible and strategically significant export channel. Qatarâ€™s heavy reliance on the Strait for LNG exports makes the closure a direct threat to an export route with no practical alternative of comparable scale. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), disruptions to transit through the Strait have reduced LNG supplies from Qatar and the UAE by more than 300 m cubic metres per day since 1 March, equivalent to more than 2 bn cubic metres per week, highlighting the scale of the shock to global gas supply.
  • The closure has also transformed Qatarâ€™s LNG challenge from a maritime shipping issue into a contractual supply disruption. QatarEnergy declared force majeure on affected LNG contracts, meaning certain delivery obligations could no longer be fulfilled under normal contractual terms due to circumstances beyond the supplierâ€™s control. This directly affects buyers linked to Qatarâ€™s export network across major Asian and European markets.
  • The implications extend beyond the decline in export revenues to a broader reshaping of buyer behaviour in global LNG markets. Importers may be forced to secure replacement cargoes from alternative suppliers such as the United States, Australia, Malaysia, Indonesia, Oman, Nigeria, Algeria, and Russia, depending on cargo availability, contract flexibility, pricing, shipping routes, and regasification capacity. At the same time, the IEA estimates that global LNG supply has fallen by around 20% due to the disruption, intensifying competition for spot and replacement cargoes.
  • This has translated directly into upward pressure on global gas prices. According to the IEA, the Dutch TTF benchmark for European natural gas prices rose by more than 45% between late February and early May. Oxford Economics also notes that gas prices continued to rise amid ongoing geopolitical tensions, although they remained below the peak levels recorded in March. As a result, the Strait closure has become a key driver of price pressures, not only because of supply shortages, but also due to the rising geopolitical risk premium embedded in global LNG markets.
  • For Qatar, Oxford Economics suggests that the continued closure of the Strait, despite the ceasefire broadly holding, points to a slower recovery in Qatarâ€™s gas exports. The crisis is also linked to delays in the North Field expansion project, even as Qatar had previously raised its LNG production capacity target to 142 m tonnes per annum by 2030, compared with around 77 mtpa currently. This highlights an important contradiction: in the near term, Qatarâ€™s inability to export oil and gas brings hydrocarbon revenues to a halt, yet higher global oil and gas prices are expected to help offset part of the lost revenue once exports resume.

Summary_EN: • Protected greenhouse productivity rebounded in 2025, reaching 58.0 tons/hectare, a significant increase from 22.6 tons/hectare in 2024. These findings highlight the strong productive potential of the five strategic crops.
DetailedAnalysis_EN: • Tracking the productivity indicator for vegetable crops in protected greenhouses between 2022 and 2025 reveals a pronounced fluctuation. Productivity declined from 97.4 tons/hectare in 2022 to 65.5 tons/hectare in 2023, reaching its lowest level of 22.6 tons/hectare in 2024, before recovering to 58.0 tons/hectare in 2025. However, this decline does not necessarily reflect a genuine deterioration in the efficiency of the agricultural sector. Rather, it appears to result from a fundamental difference in data collection methodology. It was found that the 2024 figures (and potentially those of previous years) were derived from specific controlled research trials and treatments conducted by the Agricultural Research Department for scientific purposes and were not intended to serve as national performance indicators. In contrast, the 2025 figure of 58.0 tons/hectare reflects the actual level of commercial production, as the underlying data have been validated by the Agricultural Affairs Department for the five strategic crops.

Summary_EN:
• Real GDP grew by 6.1% YoY in Q4 2024. The non-hydrocarbon GDP registered 6.1% YoY growth, lifting the headline GDP by 3.9ppt. Meanwhile, the hydrocarbon GDP grew by 6.2% YoY, adding 2.2ppt to headline GDP growth.
  • Taken together, real GDP grew by 2.4% YoY in 2024. This is 0.8ppt higher than GDP growth in 2023.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Taken together, real GDP grew by 2.4% YoY in 2024. This is 0.8ppt higher than GDP growth in 2023.
  • Non-hydrocarbon sectors drove growth during 2024, expanding 3.4% YoY, above the 2.1% pace in 2023 and nearer the 4% annual expansion targeted in Qatarâ€™s Third National Development Strategy.
  • Expansion in 2024 reflected strong performance in real estate activities, construction, wholesale and retail trade and education sectors. Manufacturing made a negative contribution to growth with growth declining by 2.2% in 2024. This is the first year since 2020 that Qatari manufacturing output has declined.
  • Meanwhile, the hydrocarbon sector grew by 0.6% YoY in 2024, contrasting the decline in industrial production. The rate of expansion was similar to 2023 and marked the third positive annual performance since 2012.
  • During Q4 specifically, construction and financial services made the largest positive contribution to annual growth, extending the trends from Q3.
  • Consensus is for Qatarâ€™ economic growth to be steady at 2.6% this year, with both the energy and non-energy sectors contributing positively to growth. The projection lies below the regional average of 3.7%. Consensus then sees GDP growth gaining pace to 5.3% in 2026, as the additional LNG capacity starts up, above the GCC average of 4.1%.

Summary_EN: • Non-hydrocarbon receipts stood at QAR 25.8bn in Q2 2025, registering a 37.5% increase relative to Q2 2024.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Non-hydrocarbon revenue accounted for 43.1% of overall revenue in Q2 2025, marking a record high share.
  • Non-hydrocarbon revenue collected in Q2 2025 represented 60.0% of the 2025 budget target (QAR 43 bn).
  • In contrast, for 2024 as a whole, non-hydrocarbon receipts stood at QAR 40.4 bn, declining by 6.2% relative to the intake in 2023.
  • Non-hydrocarbon revenue accounted for 19.0% of total government revenue in 2024, below the 21.3% share the government targeted in its 2024 budget. The government is targeting a share of 21.8% in the 2025 budget.
  • Non-hydrocarbon revenues continue to contribute less than 20% of total government revenue, leaving Qatarâ€™s budget among the least diversified in the GCC and most vulnerable to energy market trends. The share will likely decline in the medium-term given the projected rise in liquified natural gas export capacity. Qatar, alongside Kuwait, have yet to launch the value added tax (VAT), other GCC countries implemented the levy at 5% initially, with Saudi Arabia tripling the rate to 15% in mid-2020 and Bahrain doubling the rate to 10% in January 2022. Qatarâ€™s tax policies will be guided by the key 2030 fiscal sustainability targets. Key performance indicators include a fiscal surplus of 5.5% of GDP, while maintaining credit ratings at the current AA/Aa2 level.

DetailedAnalysis_EN:

Summary_EN: Total exports reached QAR 116.9 bn in Q2-2024, down by 2.4% compared to last quarter but up 6.1%, compared to a year ago.

Gas and crude oil exports saw declines both YoY and QoQ bases, while non-crude oil saw some increase by 7.1% in Q2-2024 compared to last quarter. The declines were in spite of Brent oil increases compared both to last quarter and last year, which could indicate either lower production or lower demand. Re-exports did not show any significant pattern of change remaining in the region of QAR 3-3.5 bn over the last several quarters. Exports of other goods represent 11.3% of total goods exports in Q2-2024 and exhibit a correlation of around 80% with oil-related exports, indicating that these exports are also dependent on oil-related inputs

  • Services exports saw an impressive YoY increase in Q2-2024 by 28.3% but slightly lower compared to last quarter by 0.7%. After a rather strong Q1-2024, air arrivals dropped by 24% compared to last quarter but still up by 11.2% compared to a year ago, reaching 585,655 visitors. Land arrivals followed a similar pattern, after a particular strong Q1-2024, with decline by 34.4% in Q2-2024 but up 20.2% compared to a year ago, reaching 417,291 visitors. Sea arrivals followed the seasonal pattern of decreased Q2 arrivals

According to the US Energy Information Administration, they expect the Brent crude oil spot price to average USD 82 per barrel in Q4-2024 and average USD 84 per barrel in 2025, indicating a rather flattish outlook for Qatarâ€™s exports given current production

Summary_EN:
• In Q4 2025, the number of licensed healthcare professionals reached 58,501, reflecting a 2.0% increase from the previous quarter and an 8.2% increase over the course of 2025. This figure surpasses the 2025 linear projection of 53.3 thousand practitioners.
  • On a quarterly basis, the private sector recorded an average growth rate of approximately 3%, while the public and semi-public sectors remained broadly stable, with growth rates of 1.3% and 1.6%, respectively. Over 2025, expansion in the private sector was the fastest, with growth of 12.7%, followed by the semi-public sector at 10.7% and the public sector at 5.2%.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• In total, 32,624 professionals were employed in the public sector (including both core and other public entities), accounting for 55.8% of the workforce, compared with 56.1% in Q3 2025. The private sector employed 22,150 professionals, representing 37.9% of the total workforce, up from 37.5% in Q3 2025. Additionally, 3,727 professionals were employed in the semi-public sector, accounting for 6.4% of the workforce, unchanged from Q3 2025.
  • The number of physicians increased from 9,946 in Q3 2025 to 10,030 in Q4 2025, representing growth of 0.8%. Similarly, the number of dentists rose from 2,347 to 2,390 (1.8%), while the number of nurses increased to 28,142 (1.9%). The number of pharmacists also grew to 4,744 (1.9%), and allied healthcare professionals reached 13,195, reflecting a higher quarterly growth rate of 3.0%.
  • Qatarâ€™s healthcare workforce continues to rely substantially on expatriate professionals.
