Summary_EN:
• Vessel transit activity through the Strait of Hormuz increased from 2,295 calls in January 2026 to 2,658 calls in February 2026.
  • Vessel calls then declined sharply to 158 calls in March 2026 before increasing slightly to 203 calls in April 2026.
  • For Qatar, the disruption represents a significant export-continuity risk due to the countryâ€™s heavy reliance on maritime transport through the Strait of Hormuz.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Data from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) indicates that vessel transit activity through the Strait of Hormuz remained healthy in January and February 2026, increasing from 2,295 calls to 2,658 calls. This suggests the Strait was still functioning normally before the conflict-related closure.
  • The sharp break occurred in March 2026, when vessel calls collapsed to only 158, representing a 94.1% month-on-month decline. Although activity improved slightly to 203 calls in April 2026, this remained far below the pre-disruption level. Com-pared with February, vessel calls in April were still lower by around 92.4%, indicating that maritime activity through the Strait continued to operate at severely reduced levels.
  • These disruptions coincided with broader energy supply pressures highlighted by the International Energy Agency (IEA), which estimated that cumula-tive oil supply losses from Middle Eastern produc-ers exceeded 1 bn barrels, with more than 14 m barrels per day (mb/d) of oil production shut in while tanker traffic through Hormuz remained re-stricted. The IEA also noted that around 80% of oil and petroleum product flows transiting the Strait in 2025 were destined for Asian markets, under-scoring the Straitâ€™s critical role in supporting Asian energy security and industrial supply chains.
  • The slight increase in vessel activity between March and April should therefore not be inter-preted as a recovery, but rather as a limited re-bound from extremely low levels. Overall shipping activity through the Strait remained significantly below normal operating conditions.
  • For Qatar, the sharp decline in vessel calls should be viewed as an early warning signal of pressure on export continuity. LNG and petroleum gases are the most exposed sectors because they depend on specialized vessels and uninterrupted maritime ac-cess. Ammonia and fertilizers are also highly ex-posed, given their reliance on maritime transport to reach global markets. Although helium and rare gases may have greater logistical flexibility, they remain affected by regional shipping constraints and limitations in port access.

Summary_EN: The trade surplus spanning goods and services stood at QAR 52.4 bn in Q1 2025, widening from a surplus of QAR 46.1 bn in Q4 2024 and marking the largest quarterly surplus since Q2 2024.

The surplus in goods was larger in Q1 2025 relative to the same quarter in 2024, though this was partly offset by a larger deficit on the services account.
  • The QoQ improvement in the trade surplus in goods and services in Q1 2025 was driven by a significant widening in the goods surplus to QAR 58.8 bn, from QAR 53.7 bn in Q4 2024, both on account of higher exports and weaker imports. The QoQ narrowing in the services deficit in Q1 also contributed to the overall improvement in the trade surplus spanning goods and services during the quarter. The services balance showed a deficit of QAR 6.4 bn in Q1 2025 versus a deficit of QAR 7.6 bn in Q4 2024. Lower services outgoings were the primary driver of the narrowing of the services deficit in Q1.
  • The YoY deterioration in the broader current account in Q1 2025 also reflected a widening in the deficit on the primary income account to QAR 9 bn, from QAR 5.8 bn in Q1 2024, owing to larger investment payouts. The secondary income account registered a slightly smaller deficit.
  • In QoQ terms, the improvement in the broader current account also reflected a significant narrowing in the deficit on the primary income account to QAR 9 bn, from QAR 14.5 bn in Q4 2024. This was offset by more than doubling in the deficit on the secondary income account to QAR 11.8 bn, from QAR 5.5 bn in Q4 2024, also improved markedly, with the deficit narrowing to QAR 37.1 bn in 2024, from QAR 51 bn in 2023 as inflows fell and outflows rose.

Total expenditure in 2026 is budgeted at QAR 220.8bn, representing the highest level across the three-year period and an increase of approximately QAR 11bn (5.2%) from 2025.

The 2026 allocation remains weighted toward recurrent expenditure, with salaries and current expenditure together accounting for roughly two-thirds of the total budget. At the same time, major projects retain a substantial share, indicating continued investment in strategic development priorities alongside ongoing government operating commitments.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
The 2026 budget totals QAR 221bn, up from QAR 210bn in 2025. This indicates continued fiscal expansion in the planned expenditure envelope.

Current expenditure is the largest component at approximately QAR 81bn, or around 37% of total expenditure. This reflects the scale of recurring government obligations, including operational costs, service delivery, procurement, maintenance, and other day-to-day commitments.

Salaries account for approximately QAR 70bn, representing around 32% of the 2026 budget. This confirms that workforce-related commitments remain a major driver of government expenditure and require continued focus on efficiency, productivity, and workforce planning.

Major projects are allocated approximately QAR 63bn, or around 29% of total expenditure. Maintaining this level of capital allocation suggests that strategic infrastructure, development, and transformation initiatives remain protected within the 2026 budget.

Minor capital expenditure remains comparatively limited at approximately QAR 7bn, accounting for around 3% of total expenditure. This indicates that most capital spending is concentrated in larger strategic projects rather than smaller-scale asset upgrades or localized works.

Recurrent expenditureâ€”salaries and current expenditureâ€”accounts for roughly 68% of the 2026 budget, while capital expenditure accounts for approximately 32%. The fiscal risk is that sustained growth in recurrent commitments can reduce budget flexibility over time unless matched by stronger revenue performance, efficiency measures, or reprioritisation of lower-impact expenditure.

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and related conflict disruption has shifted Qatarâ€™s LNG situation from a shipping-route issue into a contractual supply disruption. QatarEnergy has already declared force majeure on some affected LNG contracts, meaning certain delivery obligations cannot be fulfilled under normal contractual terms due to events outside the supplierâ€™s control.

This directly affects LNG buyers linked to Qatarâ€™s export network, including major Asian and European markets. In practical terms, affected buyers may need to secure replacement cargoes from alternative LNG exporters such as the United States, Australia, Malaysia, Indonesia, Oman, Nigeria, Algeria, and Russia, depending on cargo availability, contract flexibility, pricing, shipping routes, and regasification capacity.

The impact is therefore wider than export-value loss. It creates three layers of pressure: lower shipment flows, contractual delivery disruption, and buyer diversification pressure. Even if Qatar remains a critical long-term LNG supplier, a prolonged disruption could push buyers to temporarily increase reliance on other producers or portfolio suppliers to reduce exposure to Hormuz-dependent supply routes.

Qatarâ€™s HS 2804 helium / rare gases exports are concentrated in six main destination markets: France, United States of America, Japan, United Arab Emirates, China, and Germany, with all other countries grouped as Others. Unlike LNG, which is mainly an energy-security export stream, helium and rare gases are smaller in value but strategically important because they support high-value sectors such as medical imaging, semiconductors, aerospace, advanced manufacturing, fiber optics, and scientific research.

The destination profile shows that Qatarâ€™s helium-related exports are linked to advanced industrial economies and technology supply chains. France and the United States represent major Western demand centers, while Japan, China, and Germany reflect industrial and high-technology demand. The UAE may also act as a regional destination or logistics hub. This makes the indicator useful not only for tracking export value, but also for monitoring Qatarâ€™s contribution to sensitive global supply chains.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
Qatarâ€™s helium / rare gases export profile under HS 2804 is strategically different from bulk energy commodities. Although the export value is much smaller than LNG or petroleum gases, the importance of helium lies in its scarcity, limited substitutability, and downstream industrial dependence. Helium is used in sectors where supply disruption can have consequences beyond trade value, especially in MRI systems, semiconductor production, aerospace, defense-related technologies, cryogenics, and scientific laboratories.

The monthly breakdown by country is valuable because helium-related shipments can be irregular. Movements may vary due to specialized container availability, contract delivery schedules, batch shipments, and destination-specific industrial demand. Therefore, month-to-month volatility should be interpreted carefully. A single monthly drop may reflect shipment timing rather than demand weakness, while repeated declines across multiple months may signal logistics constraints, production changes, or disruption in export flows.

The concentration of exports to France, the United States, Japan, UAE, China, and Germany indicates that Qatarâ€™s helium-related exports are connected to both Western and Asian advanced industrial systems. This gives Qatar strategic relevance beyond traditional hydrocarbon markets. In a disruption scenario, such as regional maritime instability, the impact may not be measured only by lost export value; it may also affect downstream industries that depend on reliable helium and rare gas supply.

From a route-risk perspective, helium and rare gases may have more logistics flexibility than LNG because they can be moved in specialized ISO containers and may use sea, land, or air depending on urgency, destination, and volume. However, Qatarâ€™s outbound export system still remains exposed to regional logistics conditions and maritime access.

Summary_EN:
• Qatar is one of the worldâ€™s leading exporters of liquefied natural gas (LNG), helium, fertilizers, aluminium, and petrochemicals transported through the Strait of Hormuz. As a result, disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz affect not only Qatarâ€™s export revenues, but also the reliability of global energy supply chains and agricultural input markets.
  • Qatari LNG accounts for approximately 20% of global LNG trade, while Qatarâ€™s share of global helium and rare gases supply exceeds 30%.
  • Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz have led to higher LNG prices, placing additional pressure on import-dependent economies, particularly in Asia and Europe. These tensions have also contributed to rising shipping costs and maritime insurance premiums, while exacerbating risks to energy security, food security, inflation, global supply chain stability, and geopolitical stability.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Qatar plays a major role in global supply chains for strategic commodities that rely heavily on maritime transit through the Strait of Hormuz. Liquefied natural gas (LNG) alone accounts for around 20% of global LNG trade in 2025.
  • For importing countries, the Strait of Hormuz crisis has created uncertainty regarding cargo availability, delivery schedules, and replacement supply options. This is particularly critical for LNG, which depends on specialized vessels, terminals, and long-term commercial arrangements, making disrupted volumes difficult to replace in the short term.
  • Qatari LNG supports power generation, industrial activity, and energy security across several major importing markets. With the closure of the Strait, buyers may face tighter supply conditions, increased spot market competition, and greater reliance on alternative suppliers. This could drive LNG prices higher and increase electricity generation costs, particularly in countries with limited domestic supply or limited fuel-switching capacity. Even countries that do not directly import from Qatar may still be affected through higher global prices.
  • Qatarâ€™s share of global helium and rare gases supply exceeds 30%, supporting critical industries including semiconductors, aerospace, electronics, and medical technologies.
  • Qatar accounts for approximately 11% of global Sulphur supply, making it an important supplier of one of the worldâ€™s most widely used industrial chemicals, which is currently facing significant challenges amid the Strait of Hormuz crisis. Around half of global seaborne Sulphur trade transits through the Strait of Hormuz. Sulphuric acid is used not only in fertilizer and chemical production, but also in petroleum refining and the processing of critical minerals such as copper, nickel, and zinc.
  • Sulphur is typically transported by bulk cargo vessels, and shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have declined sharply since the beginning of the Iran conflict. According to Kpler commodity analytics data, only 30 thousand metric tons reached the Strait in April 2026 and 180 thousand tons in March 2026, marking a significant decline from the average monthly level of 1.27 mn tons recorded during the three months preceding the regional escalation.
  • GCC countries collectively produce around 8% of global aluminium supply, with nearly 5 mn tonnes shipped annually through the Strait of Hormuz. Aluminium remains a critical input for the energy, construction, automotive, and manufacturing sectors.
  • According to Oxford Economics, nearly 50% of regional aluminium smelting capacity is currently offline, representing approximately 4â€“5% of global supply, with supply disruptions potentially extending through 2027.
  • Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz could also increase LNG and fertilizer prices, raise maritime insurance premiums and shipping costs, and delay cargo deliveries, creating additional pressure on global energy markets, industrial supply chains, and global food security.

As shipping volumes through the Strait collapsed, markets rapidly repriced energy supply risks.

This shock translated immedi-ately into higher commodity prices, particularly in energy markets, as Brent crude prices surged from $72/bbl at the end of February to $118/bbl by the end of March, marking the largest monthly in-crease on record.
  • Oil prices also fell by about 3% on March 16 after some vessels managed to transit the Strait of Hormuz, highlighting the direct relationship be-tween market prices and access through the Strait. By the end of March, analysts had raised their av-erage 2026 Brent forecast to $82.85/bbl, approxi-mately 30% higher than the pre-war February fore-cast of $63.85/bbl.

Summary_EN:
The Strait of Hormuz closure has escalated into a global commodity shock, with March 2026 World Bank data showing sharp price increases led by energy (+41.64%) and fertilizers (+26.24%).

The impact is already spreading beyond oil and gas into food, agriculture, and wider input costs, signaling broader inflationary pressure across global supply chains.
DetailedAnalysis_EN: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has moved beyond a regional shipping disruption and become a broader global commodity shock. World Bank price data for March 2026 shows the clearest first-round impact in energy and fertilizer markets: the energy index rose 41.64% month on month, while fertilizers rose 26.24%. Food prices were up 2.74%, non-energy prices rose 2.53%, and agriculture increased 1.49%, indicating that the shock is already transmitting beyond oil and gas into wider input costs and inflation-sensitive sectors. The World Bank notes that the March surge was driven by sharp increases in European natural gas and crude oil, while fertilizer markets also tightened materially.

Summary_EN: Qatarâ€™s helium position is strategically significant, not because helium rivals LNG in total value, but because Qatar sits at the center of a small, concentrated, and high-impact global supply chain. The latest USGS estimate puts Qatar at 63 million mÂ³ in 2025e, or about 33.2% of world output, making it the second-largest producer globally after the United States. This gives Qatar an outsized role in supporting advanced sectors such as semiconductors, MRI, fibre optics, aerospace, and other specialized industrial applications.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
From a Qatar perspective, helium is not a standalone commodity story; it is an extension of the North Field and Ras Laffan industrial ecosystem. QatarEnergy LNG states that helium is produced from the North Field gas system through its Ras Laffan helium plants, and that the scale of the reservoir gives Qatar a long-term supply advantage. USGS also identifies Qatar as holding the largest major helium deposit outside the United States, at 10.1 billion cubic meters of identified resources, ahead of Algeria and Russia.

The strategic implication is that Qatar is not just participating in the helium market; it is one of the system-defining suppliers. That matters because helium serves sectors with high technological and operational sensitivity. USGS lists major uses in controlled atmospheres, fibre optics, semiconductors, MRI, aerospace, welding, diving, leak detection, and specialty gases, and notes that nothing substitutes for helium in cryogenic applications requiring extremely low temperatures. In practice, this means supply interruptions do not affect all industries equally: medical imaging, advanced electronics, and aerospace are far more exposed than lower-value discretionary uses.

For Qatar itself, the importance of helium is therefore strategic and reputational as much as commercial. A stable helium position reinforces Qatarâ€™s image as a dependable supplier of critical inputs to global high-tech and medical industries. A disruption, by contrast, would not hit the Qatari economy on the same scale as LNG, but it would quickly affect Qatarâ€™s role in critical international supply chains and expose the dependence of helium exports on uninterrupted gas processing and logistics. Reuters reported in March 2026 that when Qatarâ€™s gas processing was disrupted, helium prices rose sharply because helium supply falls directly when LNG-linked processing is interrupted.

In leadership terms, the message is this: helium gives Qatar strategic leverage disproportionate to its size as a commodity. It is a niche product, but one tied to some of the worldâ€™s most sensitive and future-facing industries. That makes helium important not mainly as a revenue line, but as part of Qatarâ€™s broader role in global resilience, industrial continuity, and strategic supply security

  • Gross loans for Qatari banks registered a growth of 1.3% in Q2 2024. Compared to 3.1% for Saudi banks, and 2% growth in both Omani and Kuwaiti banks

Summary_EN:
• Real GDP grew by 6.1% YoY in Q4 2024. The non-hydrocarbon GDP registered 6.1% YoY growth, lifting the headline GDP by 3.9ppt. Meanwhile, the hydrocarbon GDP grew by 6.2% YoY, adding 2.2ppt to headline GDP growth.
  • Taken together, real GDP grew by 2.4% YoY in 2024. This is 0.8ppt higher than GDP growth in 2023.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Taken together, real GDP grew by 2.4% YoY in 2024. This is 0.8ppt higher than GDP growth in 2023.
  • Non-hydrocarbon sectors drove growth during 2024, expanding 3.4% YoY, above the 2.1% pace in 2023 and nearer the 4% annual expansion targeted in Qatarâ€™s Third National Development Strategy.
  • Expansion in 2024 reflected strong performance in real estate activities, construction, wholesale and retail trade and education sectors. Manufacturing made a negative contribution to growth with growth declining by 2.2% in 2024. This is the first year since 2020 that Qatari manufacturing output has declined.
  • Meanwhile, the hydrocarbon sector grew by 0.6% YoY in 2024, contrasting the decline in industrial production. The rate of expansion was similar to 2023 and marked the third positive annual performance since 2012.
  • During Q4 specifically, construction and financial services made the largest positive contribution to annual growth, extending the trends from Q3.
  • Consensus is for Qatarâ€™ economic growth to be steady at 2.6% this year, with both the energy and non-energy sectors contributing positively to growth. The projection lies below the regional average of 3.7%. Consensus then sees GDP growth gaining pace to 5.3% in 2026, as the additional LNG capacity starts up, above the GCC average of 4.1%.

Summary_EN:

  • Non-hydrocarbon exports stood at QAR 38.5 bn in Q1-2025. Non-hydrocarbon exports fell by 2.0% QoQ in Q1-025, while it was 14.9% YoY lower than in Q1-2024.
  • The build-out in liquified natural gas capacity and the rise in its exports will be a key driver of growth in total exports in 2026 and 2027.

Summary_EN: Headline inflation averaged 0.7% in Q3, down from 0.9% in Q2, marking the lowest quarterly reading since early 2021
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Recreation and culture prices have been the main drivers of upward pressure on inflation this year, underpinned by strong demand associated with buoyant tourism activity. The housing and utilities category is the main drag on annual inflation and with rents continuing to adjust downward, the negative contribution will extend in the near-term. Net of housing and utilities, inflation averaged 1.8% in Q3 and 2.4% year-to-date, with higher cost of education counterbalanced by lower prices of hotel accommodation
  • Recent regional inflation readings show aside from Qatar, inflation is below 1% in Bahrain and Oman. In Saudi Arabia, the regionâ€™s largest economy, inflation spiked to a year high of 2% in November, driven almost exclusively by upward pressure from housing rents. High demand for housing will likely sustain double-digit annual increases in costs in the foreseeable future
  • Qatar Central Bank has delivered slightly deeper rates cuts than the US Federal Reserve in the current cycle. The QCB has cut its key interest rates by a total of 85bps (55bps in September and 30bps in November) versus the cumulative 75bp reduction implemented by the US Fed. After the November decision, Qatarâ€™s deposit rate stands at 4.90%, the lending rate at 5.40% and the repo rate at 5.15%. The riyalâ€™s peg to the dollar is a constraint on how much Qatar Central Bank can deviate from the Fed and its likely moves will echo those of the US Fed in the coming months

Summary_EN: • In 2022, the Out-of-Pocket Expenditure as Percentage of Current Health Expenditure increased by 3.4% as compared to the previous year. This is likely due to increased activities from FIFA World Cup 2022.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• The increase in out-of-pocket expenditure from 6.56% in 2021 to 10% in 2022 infers a growing financial burden on an average Qatari citizen and resident, likely due to privatization and changes in the national insurance system.
  • Privatization and the introduction of national insurance could be shifting the health system towards private financing, leading to higher direct payments and reduced public sector coverage, while HMC appointments backlog indicates accessibility challenges, and long-term financial sustainability concerns if the system fails to maintain balance between private and public healthcare.

Summary_EN: The ratio of non-hydrocarbon revenue to non-hydrocarbon GDP stood at 4.5% in Q3 2025.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• The Q3 2025 ratio is lower than the 7.1% in the corresponding period of 2024 and below the 6.7% average recorded in the respective quarters of 2019-2023.
  • The 2026 budget does not introduce new measures to raise non-hydrocarbon revenue, such as the introduction of VAT. Qatar, alongside Kuwait, have yet to launch the VAT, other GCC countries implemented the levy at 5% initially, with Saudi Arabia tripling the rate to 15% in mid-2020 and Bahrain doubling the rate to 10% in January 2022. Oman and the UAE have maintained the 5% VAT rate.

Summary_EN:
• In Q4 2024, private hospitals maintained their share of total hospital bed capacity at 18%, unchanged from Q3 2024.
  • Although the public sector share increased slightly during the quarter, from 72% to 73%, this shift was offset by a corresponding decline in the semi-public sector, which fell from 10% to 9%.
  • As a result, the private sectorâ€™s proportional contribution remained stable, indicating a redistribution of bed allocation rather than a direct change in private sector capacity.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• The steady 18% share of private hospital beds in Q4 2024 highlights the private sectorâ€™s sustained role in the national healthcare delivery system. This consistency reflects ongoing demand for flexible, personalized healthcare services and indicates that the private sector has established itself within the in-patient care landscape.
  • Moreover, the referred to stability signals a resilience of market-based financing models such as private insurance and out-of-pocket spending, which help relieve pressure on the public sector and support a balanced, diversified health system.

Summary_EN: International visitor arrivals increased by 1.5% year-on-year in January 2026, supported by strong growth in air arrivals and continued demand from GCC and regional markets. While sea arrivals declined significantly due to cruise cancellations linked to regional tensions, growth from Other Arab countries, the Americas, and Non-Arab African markets helped offset weaker performance from Europe and Asia. Overall, regional markets remained a key driver of tourism demand during the month.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
International visitor arrivals reached 646,266 in January 2026, representing a 1.5% increase year-on-year. Growth was primarily driven by strong performance in air arrivals, which increased by 21%, while land arrivals recorded modest growth of 1.5%. In contrast, sea arrivals declined by 50%, largely reflecting cruise ship cancellations associated with ongoing regional tensions.

By source market, growth was led by visitors from Other Arab countries (+16%), the Americas (+21%), Non-Arab Africa (+23%), and the GCC (+5%). However, arrivals from Europe (-11%) and Other Asia and Oceania (-2%) declined, mainly due to weaker cruise-related travel demand.

Despite continued geopolitical challenges affecting cruise tourism, the strong performance of air arrivals and growth from key GCC and regional markets supported overall visitor growth during the month. Continued reliance on regional markets is expected to remain an important driver of tourism demand in the near term.

  • Transport costs â€“ the next biggest item in the CPI, weighted at 14.6% - fell 0.6% in Q1 2024, as vehicle prices continued to ease. Prices for health services, clothing and footwear, and restaurants and hotels (together accounting for about 15% of the CPI) also fell

  •  The largest positive contribution came from â€œrecreation and cultureâ€, up 15.9% YoY. This item is dominated by airfares

  • Further, food and beverage prices rose by 4.9% YoY. This increase occurred despite a 2% YoY drop in the IMFâ€™s global food commodity price index in Q1-2024

Summary_EN:

Summary_EN: • Qatar ranked 78th out of 145 countries in the 2024 Economic Complexity Index, improving from 87th in 2023.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Total exports of goods and services reached QAR 455.8 bn in 2024, with goods accounting for 76.0% and services for 24.0%. Since 2012, Qatarâ€™s export composition has gradually shifted toward services, whose share increased from 7.7% to 24% in 2024. This trend reflects the growing role of transport, tourism, and ICT-related activities, which can support broader diversification and long-term productivity gains.
  • The limited expansion of Qatarâ€™s product base remains a key constraint on its ECI performance. Qatar added only 3 new products to its export basket between 2009 and 2024, suggesting that diversification has been stronger in services than in complex goods production. This limits the countryâ€™s ability to achieve a more sustained improvement in economic complexity.

Summary_EN: The trade surplus spanning goods and services stood at QAR 46.1 bn in Q4 2024, narrowing from a surplus of QAR 49.3 bn in Q3 and marking the smallest quarterly surplus in a year
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Using a broader definition of transactions with the rest of the world, the surplus on the current account stood at QAR 27 bn in Q4, shrinking in QoQ terms from QAR 36.8 bn in Q3, but marking an improvement in YoY terms
  • For 2024 as a whole, the trade surplus spanning goods and services stood at QAR 202.1 bn, narrowing from a surplus of QAR 205.8 bn in 2023. This marked the second consecutive year the surplus narrowed
  • Using the broader definition, the surplus on the current account widened to 138.7 bn in 2024, from QAR 132.7 bn in 2023, albeit remaining significantly narrower than the surplus of QAR 299.7 bn in 2022
  • The improvement last year was driven by a significant narrowing in the services deficit, to QAR 25.2 bn in 2024, from QAR 42.8 bn in 2023, primarily a result of smaller outflows. It marked the narrowest services deficit in the current series
  • The balance on the secondary income account also improved markedly, with the deficit narrowing to QAR 37.1 bn in 2024, from QAR 51 bn in 2023 as inflows rose and outflows fell
  • In YoY terms, the trade surplus spanning goods and services widened in Q4 2024 compared to the surplus registered in the same quarter in 2023, when it stood at QAR 44.6 bn. Although surplus in goods was smaller in Q4 2024 relative to the same quarter in 2023, this was offset by a smaller deficit on the services account
  • In QoQ terms, the trade balance spanning goods and services deteriorated in Q4 2024, reflecting a significantly smaller surplus on the goods account, only partly offset by a smaller deficit in services. The services balance showed a deficit of QAR 7.6 bn in Q4 versus a deficit of QAR 11.4 bn registered in Q3. Higher travel and transportation receipts were the primary driver of the narrowing of the services deficit in Q3
  • The broader current account displayed a second consecutive quarter of sequential deterioration. Aside from a smaller surplus on the goods trade balance in QoQ terms, there was a much deeper deficit on the primary income account owing to larger investment payouts. The secondary income account registered a smaller deficit.
  • Consensus is for Qatarâ€™s trade surplus to narrow this year amid global trade uncertainty and downward pressure on hydrocarbon prices. It is then seen rewidening in 2026 and beyond. The improvement will be supported primarily by a rise in gas export volumes. The strength on the trade in goods account underpins consensus expectations for the broader external surplus averaging 14.4% of GDP in the next five years

Summary_EN: Headline inflation was 3.0% YoY in Q1 2026, up from 1.5% YoY in Q4 2025, marking the fastest quarterly YoY rate recorded since Q2 2023.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• The largest positive contribution came from Miscellaneous Goods and Services which accounted for almost one-third of the total inflation recorded. Indeed, the inflation for the sub-index reached a record high of 17.0% YoY in Q1.
  • Smaller positive contributions came from Recreation and Culture services, along with Food and Beverages, Housing, Water, Electricity, Gas and Other Fuels, Clothing and footwear, Education, Communication, and Furnishings and Household equipment.
  • Meanwhile, the main drag to the annual inflation rate mostly came from Transport services and Restaurants and Hotels.
  • The QCB have maintained its deposit rate at 3.85%, its lending rate at 4.35% and its repo rate at 4.10% in Q1 2026. The riyalâ€™s peg to the dollar is a constraint on how much Qatar Central Bank can deviate from the Fed and its likely moves will echo those of the US Fed in the coming months.

Summary_EN:
• Sector investments increased by 51.7% in Q1-2025 on a YoY basis.
  • Sector investments decreased by 77.3% in Q1-2025 compared to the previous quarter.
  • Sector investments were below target by 92.30% in Q1-2025.
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• The sectorâ€™s investment flow dropped by 77% in the first quarter of 2025, reaching QAR 45.5 mn, compared to QAR 195.8 mn in the fourth quarter of 2024. This sharp decline is primarily attributed to a slowdown in investment across most key industries, excluding plastic products, fabricated metal products, and food manufacturing, which collectively accounted for approximately 91% of total investments recorded in Q1-2025.
  • On a YoY basis, the investment value increased by 66.7% compared to the first quarter of the previous year. Despite global economic and geopolitical turbulence, coupled with growing uncertainty, investment activity remained robust during this quarter. Notably, new manufacturing facilities were launched in the rubber and plastics sector, with a total value of QAR 26.25 mn, marking the largest single industrial investment of the quarter.
  • The fabricated metal products sector showed strong investment, with QAR 11.2 mn invested, driven by the opening of three new factories by the international aluminum and packaging company, Norwood. The food manufacturing sector also sustained its investment drive, with new facilities launched at a total value of QAR 4 mn during the first quarter of 2025.

Summary_EN: Headline inflation in Qatar was 0.9% in Q2-2024 down by 1.3 percentage points compared to Q1-2024
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Inflation in Q2-2024 stood at 0.9%, down by 1.3 percentage points compared to the last quarter. Inflation has been in a decreasing trajectory since Q4-2022 and is currently below the Fedâ€™s target of 2%

  • US inflation fell faster than forecast to 3% in June, leading investors to increase bets on interest rate cuts and pushing yields on US treasuries lower.

  • The largest increases in Qatarâ€™s CPI during Q2-2024 were from recreation and culture, up by 12% compared to a year ago, education up by 3.4% compared to a year ago, foods and beverages up by 2.6% compared to a year ago. At the same time, communications dropped by 9.7% compared to a year ago, housing, water and electricity fell by 3.1% compared to a year ago, restaurants and hotels fell by 1.7% compared to a year ago

Summary_EN:
• Private Expenditure on Health increased to 16% in 2022, an increase of 1% YoY

  • The trend is incrementally stable post-pandemic
DetailedAnalysis_EN:
• Qatar's percentage remained stable since 2018 and 2019, then decreased to 13% in 2020 before returning to 16% in 2022 while projecting trajectory of 18% for 2023 and 2024. This pattern indicates resilience in private health expenditure with only a temporary impact from the pandemic

  • The trend is likely due to 2 key factors: 1) post pandemic economic recovery and 2) demand recovery especially for elective and non-urgent health services

  • Comparatively, Saudi Arabia experienced a notable decline from 30% in 2018 to 22% in 2020, followed by a slight increase to 23% in 2021. This pattern reflects a significant move towards public health spending, but with a partial rebound that is more moderate than Qatar's return to pre-pandemic levels. Whereas, United Arab Emirates saw a sharp drop from 48% in 2018 to 36% in 2021, indicating a major shift towards public expenditure. This contrasts sharply with Qatar's relatively stable percentages, highlighting United Arab Emirates' more dramatic public funding increase
